passage: After the Friday lecture on signals, Yamini waited at the front of the lecture room until the others left. "Professor, I didn't understand anything today." The professor asked which part. "All of it, honestly. I feel lost." So the professor turned to the board and went through the first ten minutes of the lecture again, slowly, with the same examples. Yamini nodded at each step and said "okay" but kept looking at the clock. Afreen, waiting at the door for a lift home, saw the professor sigh quietly and Yamini leave with the same blank look. Neither had got what they hoped for. In the corridor Yamini muttered, "That did not help at all."

Harish,
You told me to go to Professor Sen for help with unit 3. I went. It was a disaster, and I think it was my fault.
I walked in and said, 'Sir, I didn't understand anything in unit 3.' He asked, 'Which part?' I said, 'All of it, honestly.' So he started from the beginning and explained the whole lecture again, the same slides, the same examples. I nodded. I still didn't get it, because I'd already heard it once and it hadn't worked.
After twenty minutes he looked tired and said, 'Maybe read the textbook chapter again.' I left angry. At him, at first. Then on the walk back I saw that he couldn't help with what he couldn't see. I never told him where I got lost.
Next time I'm trying the problems first and marking the exact line. Will you check my list before I go?
Arohi

qa.a: Professor Sen was likely frustrated and tired, repeating the lecture without knowing what was actually unclear.

Saurabh, since you're about to go to Dr Pillai for help, here's my warning. I'm Aadhya, and last semester I made the classic mistake.
I went to Dr Pillai's office hours with my textbook and said, 'Ma'am, I'm totally lost in organic chemistry.' She asked what exactly. I said, 'Everything after aldehydes.' That's six chapters.
So she did what anyone would. She went back to the start of aldehydes and began explaining, as she had in class. I was polite and nodded, but I got lost at the same point as before, because I never told her the point. She could see I wasn't getting it and grew a little short with me. I got irritated too. We both left annoyed.
Later I found my actual problem was one thing: I didn't know how to tell which carbon gets attacked. One sentence could have saved an hour.
So, before you go: what's your one thing?

qa.q: Where did Aadhya say the confusion started?
How did Aadhya feel by the end of that meeting?
qa.a: Aadhya felt irritated and still lost, and noticed the professor growing short as well.

qa.q: What would you advise Saurabh to prepare?
qa.a: Find the one specific point of confusion, like Aadhya's question about which carbon gets attacked, and bring an attempt that shows it.

qa.q: How might Dr Pillai have felt during that office hour?
qa.a: Dr Pillai was likely frustrated at re-teaching six chapters with no clear target and seeing no progress.

grounding: Shows a student asking vaguely for help with six chapters, getting the lecture repeated, and both student and professor leaving annoyed.
